ren-2.title: Renal physiology 2: Physiology of the nephron

bio-2.title: Bioenergetics 2: Regulation of energy metabolism (Pr Dinh-Xuan)

P1.A: Yes: urea, uric acid and creatinine are removed.
P1.B: Yes: the kidneys clear hormones from the blood.
P1.C: Yes: toxic substances are among the exogenous chemicals removed.
P1.D: Yes: therapeutic medications are exogenous chemicals the kidneys remove.
P1.E: No: blood cells are too big to pass the filter; red cells in urine are abnormal (hematuria).

P2.A: Yes: urea, made by the liver from ammonia, is the main nitrogenous waste.
P2.B: No: glucose in urine (glucosuria) is abnormal; all filtered glucose is normally reabsorbed.
P2.C: Yes: creatinine, from creatine phosphate breakdown, is a normal waste.
P2.D: Yes: uric acid, from nucleic acid breakdown, is a normal waste.
P2.E: Yes: the kidneys regulate electrolytes, so sodium is normally excreted.

P3.A: Abnormal: albumin in urine is albuminuria.
P3.B: Abnormal: glucose in urine is glucosuria.
P3.C: Normal: sodium is an electrolyte the kidneys excrete every day.
P3.D: Abnormal: red cells in urine is hematuria.
P3.E: Normal: potassium is an electrolyte the kidneys excrete every day.

P4.A: Yes: osmolarity is on the slide for blood homeostasis.
P4.B: Yes: blood volume and pressure are on the slide for blood homeostasis.
P4.C: No: calcitriol synthesis is listed under general (whole-body) homeostasis, not blood homeostasis.
P4.D: Yes: electrolyte concentrations are on the slide for blood homeostasis.
P4.E: No: gluconeogenesis in starvation is listed under general homeostasis, not blood homeostasis.

P46.A: No: gluconeogenesis is listed under general (whole-body) homeostasis, not blood homeostasis.
P46.B: Yes: blood volume and pressure are on the slide for blood homeostasis.
P46.C: Yes: electrolyte concentrations are on the slide for blood homeostasis.
P46.D: Yes: blood volume is on the slide for blood homeostasis.

P47.A: Yes: toxic substances are among the exogenous chemicals removed.
P47.B: Yes: urea, uric acid and creatinine are removed.
P47.C: No: blood cells are not filtered; red cells in urine are abnormal.
P47.D: Yes: the kidneys clear hormones from the blood.

P48.A: No: glucose is filtered but all of it is normally reabsorbed; in urine it is abnormal.
P48.B: Yes: uric acid, from nucleic acid breakdown, is a waste the kidneys remove.
P48.C: Yes: creatinine, from creatine phosphate breakdown, is a waste the kidneys remove.
P48.D: No: albumin is held back by the negatively charged filter; in urine it is abnormal.

P49.A: Yes: the kidneys regulate blood volume and pressure.
P49.B: Yes: they regulate acid-base balance (H+ and HCO3-).
P49.D: No: PaCO2 is set by breathing, the lungs, not the kidneys.

P5.A: Yes: GFR is about 2 mL per second, 120 mL per minute.
P5.B: Yes: about 170 L a day, which is the body fluids filtered about 4 times a day.
P5.C: Yes: of 120 mL/min filtered, 119 are reabsorbed and about 1 mL becomes urine.
P5.D: No: ADH reduces urine by increasing water reabsorption in the collecting duct, not by lowering filtration.
P5.E: Yes: molecules under 3 nm (glucose, nitrogenous wastes) pass freely through the filter.

P6.A: Yes: glucose is small (under 3 nm) and passes the filter freely.
P6.B: Yes: normally all filtered glucose is reabsorbed.
P6.C: Yes: glucose is co-transported with Na+ by SGLT proteins.
P6.D: Yes: basal Na+–K+ pumps push Na+ out so it does not build up in the cells.
P6.E: No: glucosuria comes when blood glucose is too high and the carriers are saturated, not when it is low.

P7.A: Yes: ADH is made in the hypothalamus and released by the posterior pituitary.
P7.C: No: ADH does not act on filtration.
P7.D: Yes: it inserts aquaporins so more water is reabsorbed.
P7.E: No: ADH acts on the collecting duct, not the proximal tubule.

P8.A: Yes: renin starts the chain to angiotensin II, a potent vasoconstrictor.
P8.B: No: ACE inhibitors block angiotensin II formation, so they lower pressure.
P8.C: Yes: aldosterone makes the DCT and collecting duct reabsorb Na+ and water, raising plasma volume.
P8.D: No: diuretics increase urine and lower plasma volume.
P8.E: Yes: ADH increases water reabsorption and constricts vessels.

P9.A: Yes: ACE inhibitors stop angiotensin II, so vessels dilate and less aldosterone is made.
P9.B: No: renin leads to angiotensin II, a vasoconstrictor.
P9.C: No: angiotensin II is a potent vasoconstrictor.
P9.D: No: ADH increases water reabsorption and plasma volume.
P9.E: Yes: ANP dilates vessels and makes the kidneys lose Na+ and water.

P10.A: Yes: renin leads to angiotensin II and aldosterone.
P10.B: No: inulin is a marker used to measure GFR; it has no effect on pressure.
P10.C: Yes: angiotensin II is a potent vasoconstrictor raising blood pressure.
P10.D: Yes: aldosterone raises Na+ and water reabsorption, so volume and pressure rise.
P10.E: Yes: ADH raises water reabsorption and constricts vessels.

P13.A: True, so not the answer: the AP starts at the axon hillock, graded potentials on dendrites and the soma.
P13.B: True, so not the answer: graded potentials vary and fade with distance; the AP is all-or-none and does not decay.
P13.C: Not true, so this is the answer: it is the other way round, graded potentials are short-distance and the AP long-distance.
P13.D: True, so not the answer: graded potentials come from ligand-gated channels, the AP from voltage-gated ones.
P13.E: True, so not the answer: Na+ entry opens more Na+ channels in the AP (positive feedback); graded potentials have no such loop.

P20.A: Sour goes through an H+ channel, not a G protein.
P20.B: Sour is an H+ channel and umami a G protein receptor.
P20.C: Yes: sweet and bitter use G protein receptors, salty an Na+ channel.
P20.D: Incomplete: sweet (G protein) is also right.
P20.E: Umami uses a G protein receptor, not an ion channel.

P21.A: Not involved, so this is the answer: the odorant opens cAMP-gated channels that let in Na+ and Ca2+, and Cl- leaves; K+ plays no part.
P21.B: Involved: adenylyl cyclase makes cAMP from ATP.
P21.C: Involved: cAMP opens the cyclic nucleotide-gated channel.
P21.D: Involved: the cAMP-gated channel lets Na+ in.
P21.E: Involved: Ca2+ enters and opens Ca2+-activated Cl- channels.

P25.A: Smooth muscle can contract without an AP (hormones, stretch); cardiac muscle cannot.
P25.B: Yes: both need a rise in Ca2+ to contract.
P25.C: Only cardiac (and skeletal) muscle has T tubules; smooth muscle lacks them.
P25.D: Myosin light chain kinase drives contraction only in smooth muscle.
P25.E: Cardiac muscle is striated; smooth muscle is not.

P26.A: Sarcomeres of neighbouring myofibrils do not fuse.
P26.B: Yes: strength training makes each fibre bigger (hypertrophy).
P26.C: More blood supply comes with endurance training and adds little mass.
P26.D: Training does not make new motor neurons.
P26.E: Adult muscle grows by enlarging fibres, not by making many new ones.

P27.A: Without action potentials the muscle simply relaxes.
P27.B: High Ca2+ drives contraction, not rigor.
P27.C: Low Ca2+ lets the muscle relax.
P27.D: ATP detaches myosin from actin, so more ATP prevents rigor.
P27.E: Yes: without ATP myosin heads cannot let go of actin, so the muscle locks (rigor, as in rigor mortis).

P28.A: Ca2+ enters the nerve terminal before the end plate depolarizes, not after.
P28.B: Yes: Ca2+ enters the terminal, ACh is released, then the end plate depolarizes.
P28.C: The nerve action potential comes first, before ACh release.
P28.D: Ca2+ enters the nerve terminal, not the end plate, and the end plate gives an end-plate potential, not an AP.
P28.E: The end plate gives a graded end-plate potential; the action potential starts in the muscle membrane around it.

P29.A: Yes: the AP spreads along the sarcolemma first, then down the T tubules.
P29.B: SR Ca2+ channels (ryanodine receptors) open after the T tubule depolarizes.
P29.C: Ca2+ uptake by the SR pump comes at the end, during relaxation.
P29.D: Ca2+ binds troponin C after it is released from the SR.

P30.C: Type II fibres have more glycolytic capacity.
P30.D: Yes: type I (slow, oxidative) fibres have many mitochondria and resist fatigue, good for distance running.

P31.B: Ca2+ binds troponin, and myosin has the heads, not actin.
P31.C: Yes: Ca2+ binds troponin C, tropomyosin moves off the binding sites and myosin heads bind actin.
P31.D: Myosin has the heads that bind actin, not the other way round.

P32.A: Both use Ca2+ from the SR (smooth muscle also from outside); this differs less than its role.
P32.B: Yes: in skeletal muscle Ca2+ binds troponin; in smooth muscle it binds calmodulin and switches on myosin light chain kinase.
P32.C: Both make force by actin-myosin cross-bridge cycling.

P33.A: After-hyperpolarization takes the potential below rest.
P33.B: Repolarization brings it back toward rest.
P33.D: Yes: depolarization makes the membrane less negative than at rest.

P34.A: Small motor units are recruited first (size principle).
P34.B: Slow fibres are recruited before fast ones.
P34.C: Yes: weak, small slow units first, then stronger ones as more force is needed.
P34.D: Slow, richly perfused fibres are recruited first.
P34.E: Aerobic (slow oxidative) fibres are recruited first.

P35.A: The twitch begins during the latent period, before repolarization is fully over.
P35.B: The twitch lasts much longer than the action potential.
P35.C: Yes: in an isometric contraction the fibres cannot shorten, so tension is highest.
P35.D: Shortening (isotonic) lowers the tension the muscle can make.
P35.E: Repeated stimulation adds up (treppe, summation, tetanus) before fatigue sets in.

P37.C: Yes: the A band is the length of the thick filaments and does not change.
P37.D: The H zone shortens and can disappear.
P37.E: T tubules sit at the sarcomere and move closer with it.

P38.A: Myelin speeds conduction; channels gather at the nodes.
P38.B: Myelin raises membrane resistance, and that speeds conduction.
P38.C: Myelin does not change axial resistance; a wider axon does.
P38.D: Yes: myelin lowers capacitance and raises resistance, so the impulse jumps node to node (saltatory).

P39.A: Neurotransmitters are made in the soma and terminals.
P39.B: The axon conducts the AP to the terminal.
P39.C: Yes: the hillock sums the inputs and fires an AP if threshold is reached.
P39.D: The Na+–K+ pump and leak channels keep the resting potential everywhere.

P40.A: Na+ makes the AP, not the release.
P40.B: Yes: Ca2+ entering the terminal makes vesicles fuse and release.
P40.C: Cl- is not the release signal.

P41.A: Yes: AMPA receptors are ionotropic glutamate receptors that give fast EPSPs.
P41.B: Metabotropic receptors act through G proteins, slowly.
P41.C: NMDA receptors are ligand-gated but slower and blocked by Mg2+ at rest.

P42.A: ATP comes from mitochondria and glycolysis.
P42.B: Structure comes from the cytoskeleton and connective tissue.
P42.C: The sarcolemma makes the action potential.
P42.D: Yes: the SR stores Ca2+ and releases it to start contraction.

P43.B: Yes: slow fibres are oxidative and fatigue-resistant; fast fibres give short bursts of power.
P43.C: It is the reverse: slow fibres resist fatigue.
P43.D: Slow fibres are smaller in diameter.

P44.A: ACh acts at the end plate, far from the SR.
P44.B: Yes: T tubule DHP receptors sense the voltage and open the SR ryanodine receptors.
P44.C: ATP breakdown powers the cross-bridges, it does not release Ca2+.
P44.D: The trigger is T tubule depolarization, not depolarization of the SR.

P45.A: Actin carries the myosin binding sites but does not bind Ca2+.
P45.B: Skeletal myosin does not bind the Ca2+ that starts contraction.
P45.C: Tropomyosin is moved, it does not bind Ca2+.

P50.A: Yes: a dermatome is the skin area supplied by the sensory fibres of one spinal nerve level.
P50.B: That describes a myotome (muscles of one spinal level), not a dermatome.

P51.A: Receptor activation happens on the postsynaptic membrane.
P51.B: Yes: Ca2+ enters the axon terminal.
P51.C: Yes: the terminal releases the neurotransmitter.
P51.D: Graded potentials are made in the postsynaptic cell.

P52.A: Yes: cations coming in depolarize the membrane.
P52.C: Cations entering make it less negative, not more.
P52.D: Hyperpolarization comes from cation exit or anion entry.

P53.A: Fewer Na+ channels do not shorten the AP.
P53.B: All-or-none holds only while there are enough channels; fewer channels change the AP.
P53.C: Norepinephrine has nothing to do with Na+ channel density.
P53.D: Yes: with fewer Na+ channels less Na+ enters, so the AP is smaller (or fails).

P54.A: Yes: a ligand-gated channel opens only when a molecule (the ligand) binds.
P54.B: It is closed until the ligand binds.
P54.C: Depends on the ion: most cation channels depolarize; only some (Cl-) hyperpolarize.

P55.B: Yes: tonic receptors adapt slowly and keep firing while the stimulus lasts.
P55.C: Falling response is adaptation, typical of phasic receptors.
P55.D: Signalling changes in a stimulus is the job of phasic receptors.

P56.A: Yes: removing the neurotransmitter from the cleft (enzymes like AChE) ends the graded potential.
P56.B: Neurotransmitters do not enter the postsynaptic cell.
P56.C: Diffusion away of the transmitter helps end the signal; less diffusion prolongs it.

P57.A: Can happen with Cl- channels, but the general answer is a graded potential.
P57.B: Yes: ligand-gated channels make graded (postsynaptic) potentials.
P57.D: Reaching threshold is not what the receptor itself does.

P58.A: Yes: receptor, then the spinal cord and medulla, then the thalamus, then cortex.
P58.C: The thalamus comes after the medulla.

P59.A: Yes: the parasympathetic system constricts bronchi and stimulates the gallbladder.
P59.C: It contracts the bladder (micturition); relaxing it is sympathetic.
P59.D: It stimulates digestion; inhibition is sympathetic.

P69.A: A fasciculus is bigger than a muscle fibre.
P69.B: The sarcolemma and sarcoplasm are parts of a fibre, smaller than a fasciculus.
P69.C: A fasciculus is a muscle bundle; they are the same level.
P69.D: Yes: fasciculus, then muscle fibre, then myofibril.

P70.A: ACh acts at the end plate, not on the SR.
P70.B: Yes: ACh opens the postsynaptic nicotinic receptors; the AP that follows makes the SR release Ca2+.
P70.C: ACh opens ligand-gated channels, not voltage-gated ones.
P70.D: ACh does not bind T tubules.

P71.A: Troponin moves tropomyosin, not the other way round.
P71.C: Yes: tropomyosin covers the binding sites on actin, so myosin stops sliding when Ca2+ falls.
P71.D: ATP hydrolysis cocks the myosin head.

P72.A: Yes: in a full contraction the H zone and I bands disappear.
P72.C: Z discs stay; they come closer.
P72.D: M lines and the A band stay.

P73.A: ATP is split into ADP and Pi; ADP is not phosphorylated.
P73.B: Detachment comes from ATP binding, not its hydrolysis.
P73.C: Yes: hydrolysis cocks the head, which then binds actin reversibly.
P73.D: The binding is reversible: the next ATP releases it.

P74.A: Yes: slow oxidative fibres are red (myoglobin, mitochondria) and resist fatigue.

P75.A: Yes: stimuli so fast there is no relaxation between them give complete (fused) tetanus.
P75.B: Incomplete tetanus still has partial relaxation.
P75.C: Wave summation is twitches adding up, with relaxation in between.
P75.D: Treppe is the staircase rise after rest.

P76.A: Muscular dystrophy is a defect of muscle proteins (dystrophin).
P76.B: McArdle disease is a glycogen phosphorylase defect.
P76.C: Tarui disease is a phosphofructokinase defect.
P76.D: Yes: myasthenia gravis is antibodies against the ACh receptor.

P77.A: Ca2+ is pumped, not passively moved, into the SR.
P77.B: Yes: SERCA pumps actively take Ca2+ back into the SR.
P77.C: Ca2+ goes into the SR during relaxation.
P77.D: Ca2+ leaving the SR starts contraction.

P60.A: Yes: carbohydrates are macronutrients, eaten in large amounts.
P60.B: CO2 is a waste product, not a nutrient.
P60.D: Vitamins are micronutrients, needed in small amounts.

P61.B: Water is a macronutrient on the slides.

P62.A: Yes: a triglyceride is three fatty acids on a glycerol backbone.
P62.B: Triglycerides are themselves lipids (fats), made of glycerol and fatty acids.
P62.C: Cholesterol is a lipid (a sterol), not a building block of fats.
P62.D: Yes: glycerol is the backbone of triglycerides.

P63.A: Yes: starch is a glucose polymer we digest.
P63.B: No: cellulose is a glucose polymer we cannot digest (no enzyme).
P63.C: Yes: maltose (glucose + glucose) is split by maltase.
P63.D: Yes: sucrose (glucose + fructose) is split by sucrase.

P64.A: No: that describes carbohydrates; being hydrophobic makes fat compact.
P64.B: Yes: fat is less oxidized (more reduced) than carbohydrate, so it holds more energy, 9 kcal/g against 4.
P64.C: Yes: a well-nourished adult meets 80 to 90% of resting energy needs from fat.
P64.D: No: it is the reverse, about 15% in men and 25% in women.

P65.A: Yes: the Krebs cycle runs in the mitochondrial matrix.
P65.B: No: glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm.
P65.C: Yes: the electron transport chain sits in the inner mitochondrial membrane.
P65.D: No: pyruvate is made by glycolysis, in the cytoplasm.

P66.A: Yes: too much of some vitamins (the fat-soluble ones above all) is harmful.
P66.B: Yes: vitamins are micronutrients, needed only in small quantities.
P66.C: Yes: carbohydrates are the major source of energy.
P66.D: No: proteins mostly build and repair; they are not the main fuel.

P67.A: No: glycolysis does not need oxygen.
P67.B: Yes: aerobic respiration is the matrix and membrane reactions of the mitochondria.
P67.C: Yes: the Krebs cycle is part of aerobic respiration.
P67.D: Yes: oxygen is the final electron acceptor, forming water.

P68.A: Yes: ribose and deoxyribose form the backbone of nucleic acids.
P68.B: Yes: carbohydrates are major sources of energy.
P68.C: Yes: they are cellular structural components.

H1.A: True: the slides credit him with great discoveries in neuroanatomy.
H1.C: True: he observed humans (gladiators) even though human dissection was forbidden.
H1.D: True: Galen was physician of gladiators.
H1.E: Not true, so this is the answer: medieval Europe took Galen as the reference; his ideas suited the Church.

H2.A: In Antiquity human dissection was forbidden and anatomy little used by practitioners.
H2.B: In the early modern period anatomy was an art, seen as useless to medicine.
H2.C: Medieval Europe allowed dissection only on executed criminals, and Galen was the reference.
H2.D: Yes: in modern history diseases became anatomical (percussion, auscultation) and anatomy chairs entered every medical school.
H2.E: The Renaissance brought great drawings (Vesalius, Da Vinci), not anatomy as the key to disease.

H3.B: Yes: the trade in fresh bodies led to murders (Burke and Hare), hence the anatomy laws.
H3.C: By then the Church was not the obstacle.
H3.D: Art and anatomy belong to the Renaissance.
H3.E: Not a reason on the slides.

H4.A: Empiricism is a method of inquiry: knowledge by pure observation.
H4.B: Holism is not on the slides.
H4.C: Yes: mechanism explains life by physical and chemical forces, existence as tangible matter.
H4.E: Vitalism is the opposite: peculiar life forces not reduced to physics.

H5.A: Yes: empiricism is knowledge through pure observation, with no higher purpose.
H5.B: Mechanism is a concept of life, not a method.
H5.C: Positivism relies on measurement, numbers and correlations.
H5.D: Teleology is the doctrine of causes and purpose.
H5.E: Theology is not a method of physiology.

H6.B: Yes: phlegm is one of the four humours with blood, yellow bile and black bile.

H7.A: Galen: blood is formed in the liver.
H7.B: Not Galen, so this is the answer: Ibn Nafis described the pulmonary circulation in the 13th century.
H7.C: Galen: each organ had faculties in a teleological framework.
H7.D: Galen: life is the strength of three forces (natural, vital, animal spirits).
H7.E: Galen postulated pores in the heart.

H8.A: Supernatural explanations are the opposite of positivism.
H8.C: The doctrine of causes is teleology.
H8.E: Yes: positive knowledge measures, using numbers and correlations.

H9.C: Yes: the Nuremberg code (1947) came from the trial of Nazi doctors.

H10.E: Not one of them, so this is the answer.

H12.A: Yes: with pathology moving to the morgue, anatomical lesions explained disease and anatomy became clinically useful.
H12.B: Epidemiology grew with statistics, not with pathology.
H12.C: Pharmacology is not the field meant.
H12.D: Physiology was already linked to disease.

H13.A: True of germ theory: the lab coat came with it.
H13.B: True: the microscope made germs visible.
H13.C: Not true, so this is the answer: germ theory is ontological (an outside cause the patient has), not physiological.
H13.D: True: Pasteur, Koch and Lister converged on it.
H13.E: True: bacteriology became its own discipline.

H14.D: Yes: contraria contrariis curantur means opposites are cured by opposites (cool a fever, dry the wet).

H15.C: Diet was a main remedy in Antiquity.
H15.E: Not used then, so this is the answer: metals came with Paracelsus in the Renaissance.

H17.B: Not a magic bullet of the time.
H17.D: Yes: insulin (Banting, Best, Collip, 1922) was hailed as a magic bullet.
H17.E: Steroids came later and were not the one meant.

H18.C: Germany was where thalidomide was made.
H18.E: Yes: the USA was spared because the FDA (Frances Kelsey) refused the licence.

H20.A: Yes: the Black Death (bubonic plague) killed about a third of Europe in the 14th century.
H20.C: Leprosy was endemic, not a sudden killer.
H20.E: Syphilis came at the end of the 15th century.

H22.A: Yes: blaming the victims (lifestyle) delayed the investigation of AIDS.

H23.E: Yes: the 1959 Meknes poisoning came from cooking oil mixed with aircraft engine oil.

H24.E: Yes: Wilhelm Röntgen discovered X-rays in 1895.

H25.B: Compensation applied to slaves, not to free men.
H25.C: Yes: the Code of Hammurabi cut off the surgeon’s hands.
